extracted.intended_audience: faculty/researchers and grant applicants preparing resubmissions (e.g., university investigators)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluation criteria for deciding whether and how to revise and resubmit a rejected research grant application, with agency-specific rules (NIH, NSF, DOE, DOD, foundations) and sample language for responses to reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common reasons for proposal rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists typical causes why proposals are not funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: administrative reasons; poor fit to the program; inadequate institutional or project resources; failure to convey 'intellectual merit'; budget not aligned with scope of work; poor presentation. Use this list to diagnose likely causes and prioritize fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider agency type before revising (federal vs foundation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different funders provide different information and opportunities after rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal agencies typically provide reviewer comments that you can respond to; many foundations typically do not provide comments or clear reasons. Check whether a program officer exists and can be consulted. Use this knowledge to decide whether and how to revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check procedural constraints before resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify program-specific limits and timing that affect resubmission viability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to answer: Are there maximum number of submissions/resubmissions allowed? Have you reached the agency's resubmission limit? Is the specific funding mechanism/RFP still available or expected to re-open? Is the project time-sensitive, and does the resubmission window work with your schedule? Note federal funding occurs ~6-9 months after resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether reviewers were right
rubrics_metrics.description: Critically evaluate reviewer critiques to determine if they are accurate, misunderstandings, or address fixable issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Were the reviewers right? Can you see their point? What did reviewers generally agree on vs outliers? Did reviewers misinterpret text/figures? Did you omit details that would have addressed concerns? Can concerns be rectified? Assess overall tone of the review and your 'gut' reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get objective outside input and reassess resources/time
rubrics_metrics.description: Before committing to a resubmission, obtain independent feedback and evaluate feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get another objective opinion, reassess your time/commitment and effort needed to address weaknesses, check institutional commitment, decide if project remains interesting/relevant, and contact the program officer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand realities of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that reviewers are human, can disagree, and panel fit affects usefulness of reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that a poor panel fit can produce unhelpful reviews; negative reviews may not cover all proposal weaknesses. Use this to contextualize critiques and prioritize changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH review criteria (Significance, Investigator(s), Innovation, Approach, Environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary scored criteria used by NIH reviewers to evaluate applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each criterion receives individual scores and contributes to an overall Impact score. Use these categories to structure responses and revisions; ensure you address weaknesses under the relevant criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH overall impact / score descriptors (1–9 mapped to qualitative labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric impact scores (1–9) correspond to qualitative descriptors from Exceptional to Poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptors: 1 Exceptional (essentially no weaknesses) through 9 Poor (very few strengths and numerous major weaknesses). Use descriptors to interpret severity of reviewer concerns when planning revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact score thresholds and funding likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance mapping impact scores/percentiles to likelihood of funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical guide: Impact score 10–30: likely to be funded; 31–45: occasionally funded; 46+: almost never funded. Percentile indicates % of proposals with better impact scores. Consider enthusiasm, weaknesses, timing, and fit in interpreting scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussed vs Not Discussed (ND) indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an application was discussed at the study section (Discussed) or not (ND).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ND status signals lower chance of funding; interpretation should guide decision whether to substantially revise or consider alternate actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH resubmission policy (one resubmission A1 allowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy limiting resubmissions at NIH: only one resubmission (A1) of an original (A0) is accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A1s can be submitted to any PA that accepts resubmissions. Review criteria follow current FOA. Policy applies to all NIH grant and cooperative agreement opportunities that allow resubmissions, including fellowships and career development awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency-specific resubmission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Different agencies have different rules and norms regarding resubmissions and responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: NIH requires a 1-page Introduction and 1-page Response to Reviewers at start of project narrative; DOD/DARPA uses a 2-step process where resubmissions are unlikely and debriefs are important; DOE provides a Reply to Reviewer Comments stage with limited response opportunity; NSF treats resubmissions as new applications and generally provides no reviewer response—previous applications should be substantially revised and some directorates require waiting periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-page introduction content and style tips
rubrics_metrics.description: What to include and how to phrase the one-page introduction for resubmissions (especially NIH).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include original title and proposal number, thank reviewers and emphasize strengths, address all critiques, use reviewer numbers (R1, R2, R3), devote space to most important concerns, reference exact proposal sections, be brief and direct within page limits, use active voice and plural 'we', avoid excessive apologies. If unsure about inclusion, ask the Program Officer and have a colleague review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for the 1-page introduction (substance and restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Required content and prohibited practices in the one-page introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must summarize substantial additions/deletions/changes and respond to weaknesses in the Summary Statement. Different application title is allowable; PD/PI can be added/removed. Identifying individual changes inline in the text is not permitted (NIH). Use current forms and provide substantive justification when you disagree with reviewers. Exceptions: some mechanisms (R25, Ts, Ds, some K applications) may allow a 3-page intro.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to respond vs how not to respond (tone and content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles for drafting responses to reviewer critiques, with examples of defensive vs constructive responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid defensive, confrontational, or accusatory language (e.g., attacking reviewer objectivity). Prefer concise, constructive amendments that either make the requested change, explain constraints with factual justification, or add clarifying text and cite section/page where changes were made. When appropriate, thank reviewers and explicitly state changes (e.g., revised design, added subheading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding when reviewer missed information
rubrics_metrics.description: How to address critiques that stem from reviewers missing information that was present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify and make the omitted information more explicit in the resubmission (cite original page), or rewrite sections so the information is easier to find; do not simply assert that it was present without changing the text to prevent repeated misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements to include when reviewers criticized Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: How to revise and respond if Significance was criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize how the project addresses a key gap in knowledge and aligns with the funder's mission. Strengthen the rationale and highlight potential impact and translational importance if applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements to include when reviewers criticized Methods/Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance for addressing methodological criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update preliminary findings if available, present methods matching aims/objectives, outline the approach clearly even for standard methods, explain design decisions, identify challenges and alternative approaches, and show feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements to include when reviewers criticized Experience/Investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: How to bolster investigator-related concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss relevant experience beyond biosketch uploads, recruit new collaborators or consultants if needed, consider interdisciplinary approaches, integrate an advisory board, and otherwise demonstrate team capability to execute the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements to include when reviewers criticized Overall Presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: How to address presentation and clarity issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improve project description clarity and visuals—add high-quality graphics, reorganize text for readability, and ensure reviewers can find key details easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make corresponding changes in the body of the proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t only describe responses—change the main proposal where reviewers will check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check and double-check that the body has been revised to reflect the responses; reviewers will look for these changes. Do not reinsert deleted content unless reviewers explicitly asked for deletion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate responses (examples of 'what not to do')
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific anti-patterns for response language and approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publish emotional tirades, accuse reviewers of bias or cyber-bullying, or demand re-evaluation of reviewer suitability. Instead craft measured acknowledgements, factual clarifications, and documented substantive changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatal flaws that warrant major revision or abandoning submission
rubrics_metrics.description: List of defects that often make proposals unfixable or low priority to resubmit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: proposed research not important or not innovative; hypothesis unsupported by pilot data or literature; literature review incomplete/outdated or non-evidence-based; project duplicates already completed research; methods unsuitable to test hypothesis. If present, consider redesign, pilot data collection, or changing direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical post-rejection actions to strengthen resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete administrative and content updates to do after rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit new letters of support, use updated templates and guidelines, update biosketches, avoid obsessing over prior critiques, and seek outside help and peer reviewers to vet revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative paths if resubmission is not viable
rubrics_metrics.description: Options other than resubmitting the same application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider: identifying a different study section within same agency, submitting to another opportunity or different funder, moving on from the project if necessary, or designing a pilot project to demonstrate feasibility before future submission. Don't throw good effort after bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation-specific strategy: cultivation and relationship-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance tailored to foundation funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because foundations may not give comments or clear criteria, cultivate relationships before/during/after application, revisit proposal after rejection, and obtain trusted colleague feedback. Cultivation of relationships is a key path to foundation success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of program officers and agency contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage agency staff to inform resubmission strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact the Program Officer for advice on whether to resubmit, what to change, and clarifications about policy or fit. For some agencies (e.g., DOE or DOD), debriefs can be important when invited proposals are rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission timing and strategic planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan resubmission in advance and align effort with review cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that grants are rarely funded on initial submission; start planning improvements immediately upon submission to make the resubmission better. Factor agency-specific timelines and the projected 6–9 month funding lag into your planning.
